title: An online shop for a florist
metaTitle: A florist shop built around this week
excerpt: A florist's shop should sell what can leave this week, not a permanent catalog of every stem. Put the promise on the product page and keep checkout short.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights, a room edited to what is here now.
caption: A shop floor arranged around what is actually in the room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a florist's online catalog?
faqs.answer: List what you can deliver or collect this week, with the day, the area, and the price, including delivery if you charge it. Custom work can have its own form. Past arrangements can sit in a small archive without a buy button.

faqs.question: When should a flower offer come off the site?
faqs.answer: Take it down when you can no longer make or deliver it. A page that stays up out of season takes orders you have to refuse. If you want the address to survive, redirect it to the current list and say the season moved on.

faqs.question: What should florist checkout collect?
faqs.answer: Collect the recipient, the address, the delivery window, the card message, and payment. Show the delivery fee in the total before they pay. Guest checkout fits a gift better than a forced account.

markdown:
A florist ecommerce website is a list of what can leave the shop this week. Stems change, and a permanent catalog of every flower you have ever arranged will send people toward work you cannot deliver. The product page should describe the bunch, the vessel, or the window, and checkout should be short enough to finish while the flowers are still the ones in the picture.

A marketplace grid assumes the object will still be there tomorrow, in the same variant, from many sellers. A florist's week does not work that way. Design the shop around the list you can stand behind on Monday, and take down what sold out.

## The catalog is the week

Start with what you can make or deliver in the current week. Name those offers in the language of the shop: a wrapped bunch, a vase on a table, a standing order, a funeral piece if you do that work. If you only do two of those, the site only has two.

Each offer needs a true boundary.

- Which days it can be delivered or collected.
- Which area, in words a person can check against their street.
- What is fixed, and what the florist will choose when the market changes.
- The price, including the delivery fee if there is one.

"Seasonal arrangement, price on request" is a phone call, not a product. You can still take custom work. Put it on its own path, with a form that asks for the date, the place, and the budget. Do not mix custom requests into a grid of things that have an add-to-cart button.

Retire offers when the week ends. A peony page in November, kept up because the URL once ranked, is a broken promise. If you want the address to survive, redirect it to the current week's list and say the season has moved on. A page that stays live and shows last season's flowers will take orders you have to refuse.

Keep a small archive only if it helps someone understand the shop: three or four past arrangements, labeled as past, with no buy button. The archive is a portfolio. The shop is the week. They should not share a grid.

## The product page is one promise

Build the page around the promise, in this order: the picture of this week's version, the name, the price, the day it can arrive, and what the recipient gets. A person buying for a dinner on Thursday needs the day before they need your philosophy of flowers.

Say what can change. "The market decides the exact tulips. The palette and the size stay as shown." That sentence prevents the angry note when the red is a different red. If nothing can change, because you are selling a specific planted vase you have already made, say that too.

Size needs a reference a person can picture. "A bunch for a kitchen table" is better than a centimeter count if your buyers are not florists, and you can add the count of stems when you know it. If the size is the price difference, show two sizes as two choices, not as a paragraph.

Add a note for the card, with a character count you will actually write out. Offer a delivery window in hours you can hit. "Sometime Thursday" creates a day of phone calls. "Thursday, 10 to 1" is a promise you can staff.

Care can be one line: water, where to cut, how long it should hold. A long essay on the language of flowers can wait below. The first screen is the purchase.

Leave reviews off unless you have a practice you will keep up. A widget of unnamed praise next to a perishable good looks rented. A short note from the shop about who this bunch suits is more useful, and you can write it on Monday with the rest of the list.

## Delivery is part of the flower

For most florists, the delivery is not a shipping plugin. It is the product. The day, the window, the address, and the fee decide whether the order is possible.

[Baymard Institute](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) reports that 20 percent of abandoning US shoppers left because delivery was too slow, and 40 percent left because extra costs such as shipping, tax, and fees were too high. Another 12 percent could not see the total cost up front. A flower order hits all three when the fee appears after the address, or when the only date left is one the buyer did not want.

Put the fee and the window on the product page for the common case. If the fee changes by neighborhood, ask for the neighborhood before the cart, or show a short table of the areas you cover. Discovering the fee on the last step is how a considered order becomes a complaint.

Cutoff times belong in the open. "Order by 2pm for next-day delivery in the city" is a rule the page can repeat. After the cutoff, the button should move to the next honest day, not fail in red after someone has written a card message.

Collection from the shop is a second method, with the address and the hours. It should not be hidden behind a shipping calculator that assumes a courier. Some of your best orders are people who will pick up on the way to dinner.

Substitutions need a policy in one sentence, shown before payment. Many florists must substitute. Say so, and say the limit: same palette and same scale, or we will write to you first. Silence reads as carelessness when the bouquet on the table does not match the picture.

## A short checkout

The checkout should collect the recipient, the address, the window, the card message, and payment. That is the order. An account, a password, and a survey are not the order.

Guest checkout fits a gift. The buyer may purchase once a year, for someone else's address. Forcing an account before they can pay adds a step Baymard's research keeps finding in abandoned carts: 18 percent of US shoppers in their study abandoned because the site wanted them to create an account. Offer the account after the receipt, if you want repeat customers to find their dates again.

Show the total before the card message is finalized, so they are not surprised after they have written something careful. Include the delivery fee in that total. If tax applies, include it when you can. The confirmation page should repeat the window and the address in full, because that is the page they will check from a doorway.

Do not add a tip screen, a donation, and a newsletter in a stack under the pay button. One optional note from the shop is enough. The person is trying to make a gesture land on time.

Payment methods should be the ones you already reconcile. Adding three wallets because a theme offered them is fine only if you have tested a real payment. A failed payment on a Thursday morning is a missed dinner.

## What not to copy from a marketplace

A marketplace is built for durable goods with stable variants. Flowers are the opposite. The grid of endless tiles, the "only 2 left" badge on a stem you cannot reorder, and the filter for every color in the rainbow all assume a warehouse.

Use a short list. This week's bunches, this week's vases, and the custom path. If you have twelve things, show twelve. Do not paginate a catalog of two hundred past arrangements with buy buttons turned off. That is an archive pretending to be a shop, and it makes the live work harder to find.

Filters for color can help when you truly have several live options. A filter that returns one result, or none, teaches people the shop is empty. If the week is small, skip the filter and write the palette in the name: "white and green, for a long table."

Star ratings, seller names, and "compare" buttons are the wrong furniture. You are not one listing among many on your own site. You are the shop. The page can say who you are in one line under the logo, then get back to the week.

Discount codes and countdown clocks make perishable work look desperate. A fair price stated once is calmer, and calm is usually the brand. If you do run a quiet standing-order price for offices, put it on that offer's page, as a fact, not as a flashing banner on the homepage.

## The Monday rhythm

The site stays honest only if someone updates it when the list changes. Name that person. Monday, or the evening before, they replace pictures, prices, and the sentence about what the market allowed. Sold-out items come off. They do not stay up with a disabled button and a hopeful restock date you do not believe.

Write a checklist and keep it with the other opening tasks:

1. Which offers are live, and which are done.
2. New pictures that match the crop you always use.
3. Prices and delivery windows for the week.
4. The cutoff, if a holiday changes it.
5. One look at the checkout on a phone, with the fee visible.

This is an operating task, like conditioning the flowers. A redesign that needs a developer for every price change will go stale in the second week. The editing has to be something the shop can do. The structure around that editing is the part worth designing carefully, so the week can change without the page falling apart.

The pictures are the fragile part of that rhythm. A new bunch in an old crop, or a phone photo dropped into a row of studio frames, makes the week look accidental. How to photograph what is actually available is the next piece: [product photography for a florist](/blog/product-photography-for-a-florist).

The public shops and brand sites already in [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) show the same bias: a clear offer, then the path to act.
